Area.evidence_source: [/page/4/Text/6] In order to shed light on why some offenders progress down the pathway towards suicide, we examined suicide attempts as focal events to investigate the psychological processes and social contexts in which life-threatening decisions were made. [/page/4/Text/5] Most of the respondents described tumultuous personal histories, 24 having experienced family break-down or abandonment as children, 26 recounting tales of physical abuse or neglect and 15 of excessive drug and alcohol use in their family homes. All reported recent personal problems. [/page/4/Text/7] Our first observation was that, as they talked about their past lives and described their hopes and plans for the future, those who had made only one attempt generally presented themselves as having more control of their lives than those who had made multiple attempts. In terms of their perceived control, or mastery, as exhibited in their spoken responses, they appeared similar to most of those who had never attempted suicide.
